topic: Afonso I of Kongo, letters to João III of Portugal, 1526

slides.title: In 1526, an African king wrote to Lisbon.

slides.kicker: A Christian king in Central Africa.
slides.body:
Mvemba a Nzinga ruled the Kingdom of Kongo, around the mouth of the Congo River, for more than 30 years.

Baptised as Afonso, he studied for years with Portuguese priests. He built schools. By 1516, the royal school had over 1,000 students.

slides.kicker: Portugal was his ally. Then demand grew.
slides.body:
Kongo traded with Portugal, and it also sold war captives. Afonso was part of that system.

But Portuguese buyers wanted more and more people. Soon, free men were being seized and sold. Even sons of nobles.

On 6 July 1526, Afonso wrote to King João III of Portugal. Every day, he said, traders were taking his people, including his own relatives.

He asked Lisbon to send priests and teachers. Not merchants.

slides.kicker: So he set up a checkpoint.
slides.body:
In October 1526, he ordered that buyers report every captive to three officials of his court.

Their job: find out if the person was free. Anyone who was would be taken back from the buyer.

slides.kicker: Lisbon’s answer: Kongo has slaves too.
slides.body:
The Portuguese king replied that Kongo itself kept people brought from outside the kingdom.

He offered to post two men to watch the sales. The trade did not stop.

slides.kicker: It went on for three more centuries.
slides.body:
Kongo’s region, West Central Africa, became the largest departure point for captives in the Atlantic slave trade.

Afonso’s letters survive. They are among the very few 16th-century documents written by an African.

slides.lead: Seeing a harm early is not enough to stop it.
slides.accent: Not when everyone around you profits from it.

slides.line: Save this for the next time someone warns you early.

caption:
In 1526, Afonso I, king of Kongo, wrote to King João III of Portugal: traders were kidnapping his people every day, and he wanted the slave trade out of his kingdom. He even set up officials to check every sale.

Lisbon replied. The Atlantic slave trade went on for three more centuries.

Why do you think early warnings like his so often go unheard?
